mcqs.question: What is the main limitation of vertical scaling that horizontal scaling avoids?
options: There's a hard ceiling on the size of a single machine, and it stays a single point of failure
It requires application code changes before it can be used at all
It cannot be used for database workloads at all
It always costs more per unit of capacity than horizontal scaling
mcqs.explanation: Vertical scaling needs no code changes and is often the cheaper first move — the real limit is that a single machine has a maximum size and, being one machine, its failure takes the whole service down. It works fine for databases; cost-per-unit isn't inherently worse.

mcqs.question: Why does horizontal scaling require the app tier to be stateless?
options: Any node must be able to serve any request; storing state locally would pin users to specific servers and break that
Stateless servers are always faster at processing individual requests
The load balancer physically cannot connect to more than one server otherwise
Statelessness is required by most cloud providers' terms of service
mcqs.explanation: Horizontal scaling only works if the load balancer can freely route a request to any node. Local state on one server would tie a user to that server, defeating the purpose. There's no such cloud-provider rule, and statelessness isn't inherently about raw per-request speed.

mcqs.question: Splitting a monolith into separate checkout, search, and auth services, each independently deployable, is scaling along which AKF axis?
options: Y-axis — splitting by function or service
Z-axis — splitting by data or shard
This isn't part of the AKF scale cube, it's just microservices
mcqs.explanation: Splitting by function or service is exactly the Y-axis definition in the AKF scale cube. X-axis is identical clones of the whole app, Z-axis is splitting by data partition — this scenario is neither. Microservices are a common real-world instance of Y-axis scaling, not a separate concept.

mcqs.question: Your app servers are stateless and sit at 20% CPU, but the single Postgres instance backing them is pegged at 100% CPU under the same load. What should you scale first?
options: Add more app servers behind the load balancer
Upgrade the app servers to a larger instance type
Add a CDN in front of the app tier
Scale the database tier — for example, add read replicas or shard the data
mcqs.explanation: The app tier is nowhere near saturated, so adding or upgrading app servers won't help — the database is the actual bottleneck. A CDN helps with static content, not database CPU. Scaling the tier that's actually out of capacity is the fix.
